211.quote_or_event: “One who performs selfless service, without thought of reward, shall attain his Lord and Master.”
211.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes true seva as service done with no desire for any return.
211.tie_back: The Kural says true duty toward others looks for nothing in return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain-cloud; Guru Arjan likewise defines real service as service that seeks no reward.
211.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
211._accuracy_note: Strong fit on service without expectation of return; Guru Arjan adds that such service leads to God, and there is no rain-cloud image.

212.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
212.explanation: In a salok of Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak joins honest labour (kirat karni) to sharing its fruits (vand chhakna) as the mark of one who knows the true way.
212.tie_back: The Kural says all the wealth earned through hard, persistent effort exists to help those who deserve help; Guru Nanak likewise ties hard-earned livelihood directly to giving.
212.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Sarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
212._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both honour effort and see sharing as the purpose of what is earned; Guru Nanak asks for giving some of one's earnings, where the Kural says the whole of wealth exists for others.

213.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
213.explanation: In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak teaches that service done here in the world is what earns honour in the divine Court.
213.tie_back: The Kural says no good in the world of the gods or on earth equals helping others; Guru Nanak likewise places worldly seva at the centre of what is honoured both here and hereafter.
213.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
213._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit linking earthly service to heavenly honour; the verse does not claim, as the Kural does, that nothing else equals it.

214.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
214.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak teaches that learning truly reflected upon shows itself in doing good to others.
214.tie_back: The Kural says only the person who understands what is fitting toward the world, and acts on it, is truly alive; Guru Nanak likewise measures real understanding by whether it makes one a benefactor.
214.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
214._accuracy_note: Strong fit on knowledge proved by benefaction; the verse lacks the Kural's stark claim that anyone else is counted among the dead.

215.quote_or_event: During a siege of Anandpur, Bhai Kanhaiya went among the wounded on the battlefield giving water from his water-skin to men of both armies alike. When some Sikhs complained to Guru Gobind Singh, Bhai Kanhaiya said he saw the Guru in every face, and the Guru praised him and gave him salve to treat all the wounded.
215.explanation: Sikhs remember Bhai Kanhaiya as the model of seva offered to all without distinction, even to enemies.
215.tie_back: The Kural likens the wise benefactor's wealth to a brimming village drinking-pond from which everyone may draw; Bhai Kanhaiya's water was given to all who were thirsty, friend or foe.
215.source: SikhNet, The Story of Bhai Kanhaiya Ji (paraphrase of the Sikh tradition)
215._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on water freely given to everyone; the source is a popular retelling of a well-known tradition, and the Kural speaks of a benefactor's wealth rather than personal service on a battlefield.

216.quote_or_event: The Sikh langar is a communal kitchen kept in every gurdwara, where free food is served to all who come. Under Guru Amar Das everyone ate together in the casteless langar, and in it all sit in one straight line so that no one claims higher or lower status.
216.explanation: The langar puts shared resources where anyone can reach them, regardless of caste, creed or rank.
216.tie_back: The Kural pictures the generous person's wealth as a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the village, where everyone can pick its fruit; the langar is that kind of open, central provision for all.
216.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, langar (and linked coverage in Guru Amar Das and Sikhism: The rejection of caste)
216._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on provision placed within everyone's reach; the langar is a community institution, whereas the Kural speaks of one generous person's wealth.

217.quote_or_event: Britannica records that Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, had apparently once assisted the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh, possibly curing him of poisoning; the Guru consistently sought peaceful relations with the Mughal dynasty.
217.explanation: Sikh memory of Guru Har Rai includes his help in healing someone from outside the community.
217.tie_back: The Kural likens the wealth of a noble person to a medicinal tree whose every part is a cure for others; Guru Har Rai's reported help to Dara Shikoh is an example of healing offered beyond one's own circle.
217._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Britannica itself hedges the healing story (apparently, possibly), and a single act of help does not match the Kural's image of a benefactor who is reliable and useful in every part.

218.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition as told by Macauliffe, the young Nanak was sent by his father Kalu with money to trade at Chuharkana. On the way he met holy men who had not eaten for days, and he spent his father's money on food for them, saying he had spent it to the best advantage.
218.explanation: This story, remembered as the true bargain, shows Guru Nanak giving away what he had been given even at cost to himself and in the face of his father's displeasure.
218.tie_back: The Kural says those who understand their duty do not slacken in helping others even when their own means have shrunk; the young Nanak helped the hungry with the only money he had, though it left him empty-handed.
218.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak (paraphrase of the Janamsakhi account)
218._accuracy_note: Next-best: the story is hagiography from the Janamsakhi tradition, and it is about giving at personal cost rather than continuing to give after one's wealth has shrunk.

219.quote_or_event: “The God-conscious being delights in doing good to others.”
219.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes the brahm giani, the one who knows God, as someone whose joy lies in doing good to others.
219.tie_back: The Kural says that for the kind-hearted, poverty means only the pain of being unable to do good; Guru Arjan likewise makes doing good to others the very delight of the awakened person.
219.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 273, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
219._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both treat beneficence as the good person's nature and joy, but the verse does not redefine poverty as the pain of being unable to give.

220.quote_or_event: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, was executed by the Mughal authorities in Delhi in 1675. He became the second Sikh martyr and is remembered particularly for his stand for religious freedom.
220.explanation: Sikhs honour Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom as giving his own life in defence of the freedom of conscience of others.
220.tie_back: The Kural says that if helping others leads to ruin, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself; Guru Tegh Bahadur paid with his own life for others' freedom of faith.
220._accuracy_note: Strong fit on giving one's very self for others; martyrdom for religious freedom is a more extreme and specific case than the Kural's material loss through generosity.
